source.title_on_document: The Impact of Generative AI Dependence on University Students' Creativity: The Mediating Role of Critical Thinking and the Moderating Role of Thinking Orientation

supplement.holds: Tables S1-S8: the AI dependence, self-report creativity, critical thinking, and AI self-efficacy scales; the outcome- and process-oriented priming statements; the thinking orientation manipulation check items; the CAT scoring rubrics; and the task instructions for Studies 2 and 3. The listing names no additional results or standard errors.

paper_design_summary: Three studies of Chinese university students. Study 1 is a cross-sectional survey (n = 142) relating self-reported AI dependence to self-reported creativity. Study 2 randomly assigned 132 students to a high-dependence condition (prime with mandatory ChatGPT use, then directly adopt ChatGPT's solutions on an Alternative Uses Task) or a low-dependence condition (prime with no tools, then use ChatGPT only as a supplementary reference), and three trained raters scored creativity with the Consensual Assessment Technique. Study 3 randomly assigned 160 students to a 2 x 2 of AI dependence (trust-game prime) and thinking orientation (outcome vs process prime), followed by the same AUT and CAT ratings.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing assigned; self-reported generative AI dependence measured on a 3-item scale
assignment.quote: Study 1 aimed to preliminarily examine the relationship between generative AI dependence and university students' creativity, as well as the mediating role of critical thinking, through a cross-sectional survey design.

participants.who: University students (including graduate students) with generative AI usage experience; 63 males, 79 females; mean age 24.32 (SD 2.15)
participants.quote: A total of 142 university students (including graduate students) with generative AI usage experience were recruited via online platforms

ai_tool.name_model: Generative AI in general (no specific tool)
ai_tool.how_used: Self-reported dependence on generative AI for academic research and study tasks; no task performed with AI in the study.

task.description: No creative task. Creativity measured with a 6-item self-report general creativity scale (adapted from Akpur 2020).

outcomes.name: Self-reported creativity (general creativity scale)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: 6 items, alpha = 0.87, 5-point Likert; the paper says it captures self-perceived creative capacity rather than performance on a task. Listed only to document why Study 1 is ineligible.

contrasts.reported: r = -0.20, p = 0.019; total effect B = -0.22, SE = 0.09, p = 0.019, 95% CI [-0.40, -0.04]; direct effect B = -0.07, SE = 0.11, p = 0.52; indirect effect via critical thinking = -0.15, Boot SE = 0.06, 95% CI [-0.34, -0.10]

assignment.what_was_assigned: High-dependence condition (priming tasks done strictly with ChatGPT answers, told AI answers are optimal; then directly adopt ChatGPT's creative solutions) vs low-dependence condition (priming tasks done without any tools; then use ChatGPT only as a supplementary reference and complete final solutions independently)
assignment.quote: A total of 132 university students (including graduate students; 51 males, 81 females) were recruited and randomly assigned to either the high-dependence group (n = 66) or the low-dependence group (n = 66).

arms.name: High AI dependence
arms.description: Phase 1: strictly used ChatGPT-generated answers for math calculation, text summarisation, and English translation, told 'the answers provided by the AI are optimal'. Phase 2: used ChatGPT on the AUT and was instructed to directly adopt ChatGPT's creative solutions.

arms.name: Low AI dependence
arms.description: Phase 1: completed the same tasks without any external tools or AI (browser lockdown, experimenter present). Phase 2: used ChatGPT on the AUT only as a supplementary reference and independently completed final solutions.

participants.exclusions: None reported. Analyzed count inferred from t(130) in Table 2; the paper gives no separate post-exclusion count.
participants.who: University students including graduate students; 51 males, 81 females
participants.country: China (single institution; the limitations say all participants came from one institution)
participants.quote: The two groups did not differ significantly in age, gender, or disciplinary background.

ai_tool.how_used: Both arms used ChatGPT during the AUT 'creative competition'. The high-dependence arm was told to directly adopt ChatGPT's solutions; the low-dependence arm was told to use it only as a supplementary reference.

task.description: Alternative Uses Task: generate as many innovative uses as possible for a tennis racket and a water pipe, framed as a 'creative competition'.

outcomes.name: Creativity index (Consensual Assessment Technique)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three trained psychology graduate students, blind to condition, rated each response on novelty, appropriateness, and fluency on 7-point scales; ICC = 0.86; mean of the three raters' scores used as the creativity index. The paper calls this 'expert-rated creativity' (p. 9); the raters could also be coded human_raters. Dimension-level scores are not reported.

contrasts.reported: Creativity: High AI Dependence 4.78 (0.66) vs Low AI Dependence 5.20 (0.53); t(130) = 4.03, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.70 (n = 66 per group at assignment)

studies.label: Study 3 (2 x 2: AI dependence x thinking orientation, AUT)

assignment.what_was_assigned: AI dependence (high: encouraged to fully trust the AI's investment advice in a modified trust game; low: instructed to exercise autonomous judgment) crossed with thinking orientation prime (outcome-oriented vs process-oriented statements)
assignment.quote: A total of 160 university students (including graduate students; 68 males, 92 females) were recruited and randomly assigned to one of four experimental conditions

arms.name: Low AI dependence / outcome-oriented
arms.description: Trust-game prime to exercise autonomous judgment; outcome-orientation statements; then the AUT as in Study 2

arms.name: Low AI dependence / process-oriented
arms.description: Trust-game prime to exercise autonomous judgment; process-orientation statements; then the AUT as in Study 2

arms.name: High AI dependence / outcome-oriented
arms.description: Trust-game prime to fully trust the AI's advice; outcome-orientation statements; then the AUT as in Study 2

arms.name: High AI dependence / process-oriented
arms.description: Trust-game prime to fully trust the AI's advice; process-orientation statements; then the AUT as in Study 2

participants.exclusions: None reported. Tables 3 and 4 notes give N = 160; manipulation checks use t(158).
participants.who: University students including graduate students; 68 males, 92 females
participants.quote: low AI-dependence/outcome-oriented (n = 41), low AI-dependence/process-oriented (n = 39), high AI-dependence/outcome-oriented (n = 40), and high AI-dependence/process-oriented (n = 40).

ai_tool.name_model: Not stated for Study 3; the creativity task is 'identical to the AUT used in Study 2', in which participants used ChatGPT
ai_tool.how_used: Phase 1 AI dependence manipulation used AI investment advice in a modified trust game (tool not named). Phase 3 creativity task described only as identical to the Study 2 AUT; the paper does not restate whether ChatGPT was used or what instructions each dependence arm received.

task.description: Alternative Uses Task identical to Study 2 (tennis racket, water pipe)

outcomes.name: Creativity (expert-rated CAT, as in Study 2)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Dependent variable measures 'the same as in the previous studies' (CAT, three trained raters, novelty/appropriateness/fluency averaged). AI availability during the Study 3 AUT is inferred from 'identical to the AUT used in Study 2' and not stated directly.

eligibility.reason: Study 2 randomly assigned 132 students (66 per arm) to two configurations of ChatGPT use on the AUT (directly adopt ChatGPT's solutions vs use it only as a supplementary reference), and blind raters scored creativity with the CAT. Both arms used ChatGPT, so the contrast is ai_design. The high-dependence arm also had a different prime (mandatory ChatGPT use on three tasks vs no tools). Study 3 (n = 160) also qualifies on criteria 1-3 if the AUT was done with ChatGPT as in Study 2, which the paper implies but does not restate. Study 1 is a survey with self-reported creativity and is ineligible.

one_line_finding: In Study 2, students told to directly adopt ChatGPT's AUT solutions scored lower on rater-scored creativity than students told to use ChatGPT only as a reference (4.78 vs 5.20, t(130) = 4.03, d = 0.70; p. 6, Table 2), and in Study 3 high AI dependence lowered creativity under both orientation primes (B = -1.35, SE = 0.09; p. 9, Table 4).
open_questions: Which arm is the treatment in the ai_design contrast: I coded high dependence (the condition the paper tests) as treatment and low dependence as control. Review may prefer the reverse if 'supplementary reference' is seen as the proposed configuration.

Study 3 does not state directly that ChatGPT was available during the AUT or whether the high-dependence arm was told to adopt AI solutions; it says only that the task was 'identical to the AUT used in Study 2'. The limitations (p. 12) refer to participants being 'explicitly told to adopt AI outputs' in Studies 2 and 3.
Study 3 simple effects both report t(77), but the outcome-oriented cells have 41 + 40 = 81 people (df 79 expected). The process-oriented cells (39 + 40 = 79) match df 77.
Study 3 process-oriented SDs (0.19 and 0.25) and d = 5.09 look implausibly small/large for AUT CAT ratings; the audit should check against the posted data.
Rater coding: three trained psychology graduate students; paper calls the ratings 'expert-rated'. expert_raters vs human_raters is a judgment call.
The Study 2 contrast bundles the instruction during the AUT with a Phase 1 priming difference (ChatGPT-only answers vs no tools at all).
notes: Critical thinking (17-item self-report scale) and self-efficacy (3-item self-report) are mediators measured by questionnaire, not scored on output, so they are not listed as outcomes. Study 2 Table 2: critical thinking High 2.78 (0.29) vs Low 3.17 (0.28), d = 1.37; self-efficacy 3.45 (0.72) vs 3.52 (0.68), p = 0.566. Study 2 mediation: total c = -0.42, indirect ab = -0.40, 95% CI [-0.70, -0.14] (p. 6). Study 3 critical thinking regression in Table 3 (p. 8) and conditional indirect effects in Table 5 (p. 10): outcome-oriented -0.18 [-0.33, -0.05], process-oriented 0.05 [-0.07, 0.17], IMM 0.22 [0.05, 0.43]. No diversity or homogenization outcome is reported. Paper text in Study 2 manipulation check reports Cohen's d = -0.60 with a negative sign despite high > low. IRB: Qufu Normal University protocol 2025093 (p. 14).
